cue.topic: Describe a skill you would like to learn
bullets: why you want to learn it
how you would go about learning it
and explain how it would benefit you

part2.model: I'd like to talk about a skill I have been dreaming of learning for years, which is playing the piano. The idea first came to me when I visited my aunt Beatriz in Seville two summers ago. She has an old upright piano in her living room, and every evening after dinner she would play slow, beautiful melodies while the whole family sat around listening. I was completely mesmerised, and I felt a little envious because I can't even read music. Ever since then, I have wanted to do the same for the people I love. The main reason is that I'd like a creative outlet. My job involves staring at spreadsheets all day, so I think music would be a wonderful way to switch off and express myself. As for how I'd go about it, I am planning to join weekly lessons at a small music school near my flat, and I will practise for half an hour every morning before work. I know it won't be easy at first, because my fingers will probably feel clumsy and progress will be painfully slow, but I am prepared to stick with it. In the long run, I believe it would sharpen my memory, reduce my stress and give me a real sense of achievement. And honestly, nothing would make me prouder than playing a piece for my aunt next summer.

vocab.example: The children sat mesmerised as the magician pulled a rabbit from his hat.

vocab.meaning: an activity that lets you express your imagination
vocab.example: Painting at weekends gives me a creative outlet after stressful weeks.

vocab.meaning: stop thinking about work and relax completely
vocab.example: It is hard to switch off when your phone keeps buzzing.

vocab.meaning: frustratingly slow, almost unbearably so

vocab.meaning: continue doing something even when it is hard
vocab.example: If you stick with it, the guitar gets easier every week.

vocab.meaning: the proud feeling of having completed something worthwhile
vocab.example: Finishing the marathon gave her a huge sense of achievement.

roundingOff.q: Do you think it is easier for children to learn new skills than adults?
roundingOff.model: Generally, yes. Children are like sponges, absorbing information with little effort, and they are not afraid of making mistakes. Adults, on the other hand, tend to be self-conscious and short of time. That said, I believe grown-ups make up for it with discipline and a clear purpose, so it is never too late to pick up something new.

questions.q: Why do some people find it hard to learn new skills as they get older?
questions.model: I think it mostly comes down to confidence and habit. Older people are often set in their ways, and they worry about looking foolish in front of younger classmates. They also juggle work and family, so there is little energy left for study. However, I don't believe age itself is the barrier. With patience and a supportive teacher, adults can master new abilities just as effectively. In my view, the real obstacle is the fear of failure, not a lack of ability.

questions.q: To what extent can online courses replace traditional classroom learning?
questions.model: To a certain extent, they can. Online courses are flexible, affordable and allow learners to study at their own pace from anywhere in the world. Nevertheless, they cannot fully replace face-to-face teaching, because many students need direct feedback and the motivation that comes from sharing a room with classmates. Personally, I believe a blended approach is ideal, with theory delivered online and practical sessions held in person. That way, learners enjoy the best of both worlds.

vocab.example: Online lessons let busy adults progress at their own pace.

questions.q: Should employers pay for their staff to receive further training?
questions.model: I strongly believe they should, because it is a sound investment. Well-trained employees are more productive and more likely to stay with the company, which saves money on recruitment. Furthermore, workers who feel valued tend to be far more loyal. Admittedly, small businesses may struggle to cover the cost, so the government could offer tax incentives to lighten the load. Overall, everyone gains when companies support professional development, including customers who receive a better service.

questions.q: What might happen to society if people stopped learning after leaving school?
questions.model: Society would almost certainly stagnate. Technology is advancing so rapidly that skills quickly become out of date, so workers who stop learning would soon fall behind and struggle to find jobs. Innovation would slow down as well, because new ideas depend on curious minds. On a personal level, people might lose their sense of purpose and become less open-minded. For these reasons, I think we should treat education as a lifelong journey rather than something that ends at eighteen.

questions.q: Which skills do you think will be most valuable for young people in the future?
questions.model: I would say adaptability and digital literacy will be crucial. Since many of today's jobs may be automated, young people will need to retrain several times during their careers. Alongside technical know-how, soft skills such as teamwork and critical thinking will set candidates apart, because machines cannot easily copy them. In my opinion, schools should therefore focus less on memorising facts and more on teaching students how to learn independently.

questions.q: How far is practical experience more useful than formal qualifications?
questions.model: It depends on the field. In careers like surgery or engineering, formal qualifications are non-negotiable because mistakes can be extremely costly. In creative industries, however, a strong portfolio often speaks louder than a certificate. Personally, I think hands-on experience teaches things no textbook can, such as working under pressure. Even so, qualifications open doors in the first place, so the ideal situation is to gain both side by side, learning on the job while studying.
